#9723. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:

Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It shows how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

Linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

CatBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

One caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:

Up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

Out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

More data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

The full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

#9722. AI Made Us Faster. So Why Do Designers Have Less Time?

Art director and brand designer. Ex-Avito, ivi, MY.GAMES. Founder of Design Warm-ups, a 3,000+ designer community.

Art director and brand designer. Ex-Avito, ivi, MY.GAMES. Founder of Design Warm-ups, a 3,000+ designer community.

Art director and brand designer. Ex-Avito, ivi, MY.GAMES. Founder of Design Warm-ups, a 3,000+ designer community.

A poster that used to take me a day now takes a minute to generate. Last night I built an animated website in one evening without writing a single line of code. By every estimate, designers should have half their lives back.

Yet I haven't met a single designer who has more free time. Deadlines are shorter, revisions are longer, and by the evening there are so many options that your eyes start to blur.

So I tried to figure out what is going on. Are we bad at working with AI? Were we sold a fantasy? Or is this just a bubble that is about to pop? The answer turned out to be more interesting than all three.

In 2025, researchers at METR ran a simple experiment. Sixteen experienced developers worked on real tasks, some with AI tools and some without. Before they started, they expected AI to make them 24% faster.

With AI, tasks took 19% longer. The strangest part: even after the experiment, they believed AI had made them 20% faster.

The study is small, and it is about developers, not designers. But the same picture shows up in much larger surveys:

2,500 workers and executives in 4 countries

96% of executives expect AI to raise productivity. 77% of employees say it added to their workload

52 interviews, 300+ public AI initiatives

95% of organizations got zero return from generative AI

Computers went through the same thing in the 1980s. Economist Robert Solow famously observed that you could see the computer age everywhere except in the productivity statistics. The growth did come, but only after people rebuilt the way they worked.

I see three reasons, and none of them is that the models are bad.

1. Generation got cheap. Choosing didn't. A designer used to make three options and bring the best one. Now you can get 200 in an hour. Each one has to be looked at, compared, and rejected for a reason. Nobody counts that time, but it eats all the savings.

2. Clients know generation takes a minute too. So "by Friday" turned into "by tomorrow", and one round of revisions turned into five. Economists call this the Jevons paradox: when something gets cheaper, we consume more of it. Cheap images didn't reduce the work. They increased the appetite.

3. We dropped AI into the old process. Brief, references, sketches, approvals all stayed the same. There is just a new "generate" button in the middle. According to Upwork, 47% of employees using AI don't know how to reach the productivity gains their managers expect. And in the MIT report, the 5% of companies that succeeded rebuilt the process itself instead of buying one more tool.

There is one more thing METR showed. With AI, the feeling of speed and actual speed drift apart. Generating gives you the sense that work is happening even when it is stuck. For designers, it looks like an hour of rerolling one frame instead of five minutes thinking about what exactly is wrong with it.

Fair question. In June 2026, JPMorgan estimated global AI infrastructure spending at $5.5 trillion through 2030. The largest cloud providers alone are spending about $650 billion in 2026, increasingly with borrowed money. Investors argue about one thing: whether demand will catch up with the spending.

For designers, I think something else matters more. Even if the financial bubble pops, the tools won't disappear. After the dot-com crash in 2000, the internet didn't go away. The companies that couldn't make money on it did, and the ones that could grew in their place.

AI looks similar. If there is a bubble, it is in expectations: "buy a subscription and everything gets faster." The data above shows it doesn't work that way. But the change in the profession has already happened, and it won't roll back.

There is another tension in the industry. Open Threads and it looks like everyone is a designer now. The profession has ballooned and is changing in front of us. But behind a lot of those generations is a lack of basics: composition, grids, typography. AI doesn't fix that. It mass-produces it.

That is especially true for product designers moving from interfaces into visual work. A component library keeps a UI consistent, but there is no Storybook for light, texture and framing.

None of these steps requires a new model. They are all about who is running the process.

We weren't fooled. We were sold faster execution and assumed we had bought faster work. AI speeds up making things. It doesn't free up a designer's time on its own. The person who frees up time is the one who decided in advance what they are making and knows how to choose quickly.

That animated website from the first paragraph took one evening for exactly that reason: I knew what feeling I wanted before I typed the first prompt. Without that, I would still be rerolling it.

Has AI saved you time, or eaten it? And how have your deadlines changed in the last year?

AI Didn’t Kill Design. But Something About the Profession Is Changing Anyway

Art director and brand designer. Ex-Avito, ivi, MY.GAMES. Founder of Design Warm-ups, a 3,000+ designer community.

#9720. DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:

The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:

The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

We thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

Adapted from the original RadixArk article.

They do not reflect modern usage. Grammarly is much better at this.- Pro Writing Aid seems to waste their limited resources on tweaking their UI. Their UI most definitely could use improvement, but these changes are not great improvements; they only serve to confuse users. Their resources would be better spent fixing the many functional problems in their app.- Some of Pro Writing Aid's checks are completely useless, as they do not take context into consideration. For example, an ordinary word would not be capitalized as part of a narrative, but would be as part of a title (for example, "professor." But if you capitalize correctly for context, Pro Writing Aid dings you for "Inconsistent capitalization." Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.

#9717. Weekly #48-2026: Microsoft's Outage Post-Mortem, Backdoored Coding Agents, AI Code Review, PHP 8.6

Last week we talked about the Outlook outage. This week Microsoft published its final report, and it reads like a lesson in how safety systems can turn against you.

The bug came from a July update to the gateway servers that handle Microsoft 365 connections. Load tests ran on older machines with fewer cores, so they never saw it; only the newer, high-core servers were affected. Then the safeguards made it worse. Automatic failover pushed Teams traffic onto the gateway that Exchange shares, traffic management moved load from failing servers onto healthy ones, and recovering servers were overwhelmed the moment they came back. Within about two hours every region was affected.

The report lists 20 repair items, seven done and 13 still to come, including smaller failure zones, separate capacity pools and load tests on the newest hardware.

For us, two questions are worth asking: does our test environment look like production hardware, and could our retries and failover spread a failure instead of containing it?

Microsoft's security researchers just showed how a coding agent can be turned against you before you ever install it.

The attack lives in the post-training supply chain: the fine-tuning datasets and third-party model checkpoints teams pull in to customise their agents. In one experiment, the team slipped 90 crafted examples into roughly 9,000 terminal-agent conversations, about 1% of the data. After fine-tuning, the model ran unsafe commands in around 78% of trials on the harnesses it was trained on. With full control over training, backdoored Qwen models reached 84 to 95% success even on repositories they had never seen.

For us as engineers, the lesson is that a model is now a dependency, just like an npm package. Microsoft's advice reads like classic supply-chain hygiene: pin datasets by hash, treat outside checkpoints as untrusted, give agents the smallest tool permissions they need, and log every tool call.

If your team fine-tunes or downloads models for its agents, this is the week to ask who checks what goes into them.

Agents now write most of the code at Rootly, so their CTO asked a hard question: is human code review still doing its job?

He looked at 3,661 pull requests merged between August and early November. The main repo merged 356 PRs in October last year and 2,053 this October, while the number of approvers grew by just two. Over 90% of PRs were approved without a single review comment, and in 43% the last approval was on an older commit than the one that was merged.

His proposal is careful. An AI reviewer could approve only low-risk changes with a top score on the latest commit, and never anything touching migrations, auth, permissions, billing, deploy config or dependencies. The agent that wrote a PR can't approve it, and a new push cancels the approval. Even then, he says the data justifies testing the rule in shadow mode, not switching it on.

It's an honest look at a question many teams avoid: is our review a real check, or just a rubber stamp?

How do you know a change to your AI setup made it better? Until now, most of us tried a few prompts and went with our gut. GitHub's answer, released on November 17, is Copilot Evals, now in public preview.

An eval is a repeatable test for AI behaviour. You can create one for a skill, a custom agent or an MCP tool, either by asking Copilot or with the /eval command. It checks the final result and the path the agent took to get there. Because AI output changes from run to run, you rerun the same eval after each change and compare before and after. It works in VS Code, the Copilot CLI and the Copilot app.

This is the discipline we already apply to code: no change without a test. If your team keeps a library of prompts, instructions or agent skills, they deserve regression tests too.

It's early, but expect evals to become as normal in agent projects as unit tests are today.

PHP 8.6 shipped on November 19, and it's a release with something for almost every PHP developer.

The headline feature is partial function application: put a question-mark placeholder in a call and you get back a closure with the other arguments already filled in. There's a new Time\Duration class with nanosecond precision, a clamp() function, a SortDirection enum that libraries can share, and readonly properties can finally have default values. For async work, a new Io\Poll API watches many streams using epoll or kqueue and removes the old 1,024-connection limit of stream_select().

For Laravel teams the practical step is simple: run your test suite on 8.6 in CI now, and let the deprecation warnings tell you what to fix.

#9716. Setting Up AWS Control Tower? These SCP and Networking Mistakes Can Cost You Hours

Most landing-zone guides stop after "click Set up landing zone". This one keeps going. By the end, you will have a working multi-account AWS environment where every account has one job, the rules are enforced by Service Control Policies, and the network is owned by one account and shared with the others. Each rule is tested from the command line, so you can prove it holds.

Everything here was built in a real organization, including the parts that went wrong: an SCP that broke DNS, an "allow list" SCP that allowed everything, and a RAM share that failed for 40 minutes. The fixes are part of the steps and are collected in the Troubleshooting section.

This is part 1 of a series. Part 2 sets up the Build account (CodeCommit, ECR with cross-account pull, and CodeBuild inside the shared VPC), and part 3 runs the application on ECS in Dev and Production.

Seven accounts, grouped into Organizational Units (OUs), each with one responsibility:

The "must not" rules matter as much as ownership: each one becomes a Deny statement in an SCP, so it holds even for an administrator inside that account.

An AWS account is a hard boundary for IAM permissions, billing, service quotas, and the blast radius of mistakes. When dev, prod, networking, and CI/CD share one account, a developer who needs the dev cluster easily ends up with access to production, and costs can only be split with careful tagging. Separate accounts give you these boundaries for free, and OUs let you apply the same rules to a group of accounts at once: every account you add to the Workloads OU later inherits its guardrails.

The design follows one principle, ownership: for any resource, it should be obvious which account owns it and who is allowed to change it. The network belongs to the Network account, images belong to the Build account, and the running application belongs to the workload account. Images are built once and only pulled by Dev and Production, so Production runs exactly what was tested in Dev.

This article builds only Dev and Production. A Staging account can be added later in exactly the same way.

Control Tower itself is free, but the services it enables are not. Approximate monthly costs in eu-central-1 for this setup:

The NAT gateways are almost all of the bill. If you build this only to learn, follow the Cleanup section when you are done, or delete the NAT gateways between sessions.

Control Tower creates the organization structure, the two shared accounts in the Security OU, an organization-wide CloudTrail trail, and AWS Config in every enrolled account. Everything later in this article builds on it.

Before you start: if IAM Identity Center is already enabled in the management account, Control Tower must be set up in the same Region. Choose the home Region carefully. Changing it later means decommissioning the landing zone.

Sign in to the management account and open AWS Control Tower → Set up landing zone.

On the first page, choose your home Region and Automatic account enrollment. With automatic enrollment, accounts that join the organization later (and accounts you move between OUs) get the Control Tower baseline and controls without manual enrollment.

On the second page, keep the recommended Sandbox OU. It is a place for experiments with fewer restrictions, and we will also use it to test new SCPs before they reach other OUs.

Next, Control Tower asks for the two shared accounts in the Security OU:

The setup takes about 35 minutes. You can follow each step on the landing zone page:

Control Tower created the Security and Sandbox OUs. Create the other three under Root in Control Tower → Organization → Create resources → Create organizational unit: Infrastructure, Deployments, and Workloads. Create them through Control Tower, not the Organizations console, so that they are registered and get the Control Tower controls.

If you expect many workloads, you can nest OUs later, for example Workloads/web and Workloads/ai, and attach different policies to each.

Use Control Tower → Account Factory → Create account for each workload account:

Account Factory provisions accounts one at a time, so creating all four takes a while. When it's done, Control Tower → Organization should show every OU as Registered and every account as Enrolled:

Control Tower configures IAM Identity Center. It creates groups such as AWSControlTowerAdmins, AWSSecurityAuditors, and AWSLogArchiveViewers, and permission sets such as AWSAdministratorAccess, AWSPowerUserAccess, and AWSReadOnlyAccess. In every enrolled account, your user gets AWSAdministratorAccess directly, while the AWSControlTowerAdmins group only gets AWSOrganizationsFullAccess. That direct assignment is how I sign in everywhere in this article:

For a team, don't give everyone administrator access. Create groups by role and assign each group only to the accounts it needs:

In the console: IAM Identity Center → Groups → Create group, then AWS accounts → select the accounts → Assign users or groups → choose the group and the permission set. The same assignment from the CLI:

For the command line, add one profile per account to ~/.aws/config, then sign in once with aws sso login --sso-session lz. One sign-in covers all profiles:

Tip: use the role name that you actually see in the access portal. In my organization the management account has AdministratorAccess while member accounts have AWSAdministratorAccess. A wrong role name fails with "ForbiddenException: No access".

Also check that no AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID or AWS_SESSION_TOKEN environment variables are set in your shell. The CLI uses them whenever a command has no --profile, so a single forgotten flag silently runs that command against a completely different account. I had exactly this situation, with keys for an unrelated organization in my shell.

Service Control Policies (SCPs) are guardrails in AWS Organizations. They define the maximum permissions available to IAM users and roles in the accounts of an OU, regardless of what their IAM policies allow.

We use them to enforce the Region, to block dangerous actions (leaving the organization, disabling security services), to enforce ownership (only the Network account builds connectivity), and to remove risky shortcuts (root user, long-lived access keys). SCPs say "what's possible", IAM policies say "who can do it".

We don't attach our policies to the Security OU. Control Tower manages the Audit and Log Archive accounts and already protects them with its own guardrails (the aws-guardrails-* policies you can see in the list).

Every Deny statement below has an exception for the AWSControlTowerExecution role and the stacksets-exec-* roles. Control Tower uses these roles to manage the accounts, and blocking them would break enrollment and drift repair.

Go to AWS Organizations → Policies → Service control policies → Create policy, and name it BaselineGuardrails :

The Network account owns connectivity. FullAWSAccess already allows that, so we only add what it must not do: run applications or CI/CD.

The Build account owns pipelines and container images. It must not create its own network connectivity (Transit Gateway, peering, VPN, Direct Connect) and must not run application services or databases.

Dev and Production run the application. They may attach their VPC to a Transit Gateway shared by the Network account, but cannot build their own connectivity, create ECR repositories, push images, or create pipelines. Images are built once in the Build account and only pulled here.

Select the policy → Actions → Attach policy, and choose the OU:

Leave FullAWSAccess attached. Our policies only take permissions away from it.

The final picture for the Workloads OU should be: FullAWSAccess, the Control Tower aws-guardrails-* policy, BaselineGuardrails, and WorkloadsECSPolicy:

Always test SCPs right after attaching them. EC2 supports --dry-run, which checks permissions without creating anything:

The error message names the exact SCP that denied the request, which makes troubleshooting much easier. Section 7 has a script that tests all guardrails at once.

Tip: before attaching a new SCP to a production OU, attach it to the Sandbox OU or a test account first. A wrong Deny statement affects every account in the OU immediately.

With the guardrails in place, we can build the network. The Network account owns all VPCs, subnets, route tables, NAT gateways, and internet gateways. Dev, Production, and Build don't create VPCs. They receive subnets from the Network account through AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM).

One shared VPC for everyone would put Dev and Production on the same network. Instead, each environment gets its own VPC, shared only with its own account, and we don't need a Transit Gateway yet.

Before creating anything, plan the IP ranges. VPCs that may need to be connected later (with Transit Gateway or peering) must not overlap. Control Tower created a VPC in every account with the same 172.31.0.0/16 range, and these VPCs can never be connected to each other.

We reserve a /16 range for each environment:

Each environment VPC uses two Availability Zones and three subnet tiers:

The app subnets are larger (/20, about 4,000 addresses) because every ECS task on Fargate gets its own IP address. Production uses the same layout with 10.20.x.x. The build VPC needs only two public and two private subnets (10.30.0.0/24, 10.30.1.0/24, 10.30.16.0/20, 10.30.32.0/20).

Control Tower's Account Factory created an empty VPC named aws-controltower-VPC in every new account. We don't need them, so delete them in the Network, Build, Dev, and Production accounts (VPC → Your VPCs → select aws-controltower-VPC → Actions → Delete VPC).

To prevent Control Tower from creating these VPCs in future accounts, go to Control Tower → Account Factory → Network configuration → Edit, and set the maximum number of private subnets to 0.

Sign in to the Network account, open VPC → Create VPC, and choose VPC and more. This wizard creates the VPC, subnets, route tables, internet gateway, NAT gateway, and VPC endpoints in one step.

Expand Customize subnets CIDR blocks and enter the CIDRs from the table above. The wizard's defaults would give the public subnets /20 ranges, which wastes addresses we want to keep for ECS tasks.

ECS tasks in private subnets need outbound access to pull container images, send logs, and call external APIs. This is the job of the NAT gateway. The wizard offers three options:

We make a different choice per environment:

For prod, choose Regional instead of Zonal. There is no AZ selection for a regional NAT gateway, because AWS manages its availability across zones:

Choose S3 Gateway. Gateway endpoints are free. Amazon ECR stores image layers in S3, so most of the traffic when ECS pulls an image goes through the endpoint instead of the NAT gateway, which reduces NAT data processing costs.

We don't create interface endpoints (ECR, CloudWatch Logs, STS) yet. At about $0.01 per hour per AZ each, five of them in two AZs cost more than the NAT gateway they would replace.

Keep DNS hostnames and DNS resolution enabled.

Before creating the VPC, check the Preview panel on the right. It shows every resource the wizard will create. You should see six subnets, one internet gateway, one NAT gateway, and private route tables with a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the NAT gateway.

Click Create VPC. Creating the NAT gateway takes a minute or two.

Open the VPC and look at the Resource map tab. It shows the whole design on one screen: six subnets in two AZs, the public route table pointing to the internet gateway, and the private route tables pointing to the NAT gateway and the S3 endpoint.

Repeat the same steps for prod (10.20.0.0/16, Regional NAT gateway) and build (10.30.0.0/16, 2 public and 2 private subnets, Zonal NAT gateway in 1 AZ).

First, allow RAM to share resources within the organization. In the management account, open Resource Access Manager → Settings and enable Enable sharing with AWS Organizations. Without this setting, resources can only be shared through invitations.

Now, in the Network account, open Resource Access Manager → Resource shares → Create resource share:

When I created the first share, it failed with this error, even though organization sharing was enabled a few minutes earlier:

The message suggests waiting for onboarding to finish, but mine still failed after 40 minutes, from every account. The real hint came from the CLI: sharing with the organization as principal returned UnknownResourceException: Organization o-xxxxxxxx. RAM had never imported the organization, even though the Organizations console listed RAM as a trusted service.

The fix was to reset RAM trusted access from the management account:

Run this only before you have any resource shares. Disabling trusted access affects existing organization-based shares. After the reset, sharing worked within a minute.

Before that, I ruled out our own SCP by detaching BaselineGuardrails from the Infrastructure OU for a minute. A good habit in a governed account: rule out your own SCPs first. The error message names the denying SCP, as in this example where the region lock blocks CloudTrail in us-east-1:

Sign in to the Dev account and open VPC → Subnets. The shared subnets appear with the Network account as the owner.

Guardrails are easy to get subtly wrong, so I keep a script that checks the important rules in one run. It only uses read-only calls and EC2 --dry-run, so it never creates anything:

The "allow" checks matter too: a guardrail that blocks too much is also a bug, like my first region lock that broke Route 53. Run the script after every SCP change.

Every problem I hit while building this part, in one place:

If you built this only to learn, delete it in this order. Participants must remove their resources from shared subnets before the owner can delete them.

Dev, Production, and Build accounts: delete anything you launched into the shared subnets, including security groups.

Network account: delete the three RAM shares. Then delete the NAT gateways and release their Elastic IP addresses (this stops most of the cost), and delete the three VPCs.

Management account: detach and delete the four custom SCPs. To remove everything, decommission the landing zone in Control Tower, then close the member accounts. Closed accounts stay suspended for 90 days.

We now have a landing zone where every account has one clear job, and the boundaries are enforced rather than just documented:

#9715. Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:

Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

For this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:

We used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:

Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:

858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

This example shows how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

The pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:

The figure below shows how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below shows what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which showed that 0.1 worked best).

We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

Each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

The final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:

Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

We also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

The number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

Merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

We started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

We concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each update below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:

The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own update. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):

"Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

The super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

During training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets new tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

We evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi automatically applies context compaction, while OpenCode and Hermes don't, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

Every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

All three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

The adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

We appreciate the feedback from the users and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

This question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

This phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

However this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

Throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

We also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

#9713. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)


If you want to pay online, you need to register an account and provide credit card information. If you don't have a credit card, you can pay with bank transfer. With the rise of cryptocurrencies, these methods may become old.

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain. 

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

So, What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

  • Blockchain collects information in “blocks”.
  • A block has a storage capacity, and once it's used up, it can be closed and linked to a previously served block.
  • Blocks form chains, which are called “Blockchains.”
  • More information will be added to the block with the most content until its capacity is full. The process repeats itself.
  • Each block in the chain has an exact timestamp and can't be changed.

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

How does blockchain work?

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

Here’s how it works:

  • Someone or a computer will transacts
  • The transaction is transmitted throughout the network.
  • A network of computers can confirm the transaction.
  • When it is confirmed a transaction is added to a block
  • The blocks are linked together to create a history.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

  • A new transaction is added to the system. It is then relayed to a network of computers located around the world. The computers then solve equations to ensure the authenticity of the transaction.
  • Once a transaction is confirmed, it is placed in a block after the confirmation. All of the blocks are chained together to create a permanent history of every transaction.

How are Blockchains used?

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

What is Blockchain Decentralization?

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Pros and Cons of Blockchain

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages. 

Pros

  • Accuracy is increased because there is no human involvement in the verification process.
  • One of the great things about decentralization is that it makes information harder to tamper with.
  • Safe, private, and easy transactions
  • Provides a banking alternative and safe storage of personal information

Cons

  • Data storage has limits.
  • The regulations are always changing, as they differ from place to place.
  • It has a risk of being used for illicit activities 

Frequently Asked Questions About Blockchain

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Is Blockchain a cryptocurrency?

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Is it possible for Blockchain to be hacked?

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

What is the most prominent blockchain company?

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Who owns Blockchain?

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

What is the difference between Bitcoin and Blockchain technology?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency 

What is the difference between Blockchain and a Database?

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Final Saying

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). #9712. Building an All-in-One Browser PDF Editor Without Creating an All-in-One Mess

Every PDF editor seems to follow a familiar path.

Start with merging. Add splitting. Then compression, conversion, page rotation, protection, signatures, OCR, metadata editing, and eventually several more buttons nobody remembers requesting.

Before long, the simple editor has become a complicated application.

The problem isn't necessarily having many features. It's making all of them feel like separate products inside one interface.

Instead of thinking about a PDF editor as a list of tools, think about what users are trying to accomplish.

A person might want to: rearrange pages, remove unnecessary sections, combine supporting documents, reduce file size, export content into another format, protect a final document.

These operations are related. The interface should make moving between them feel natural.

For example, after uploading a PDF, a user could see a page overview with options to rearrange, rotate, or remove pages. That's more intuitive than forcing them to return to a homepage and upload the same document repeatedly.

One architecture, different processing operations

An all-in-one editor benefits from reusable components. Think about separating the application into:

File input — handles uploads, validation, supported formats, and document selection.

Document state — tracks selected files, page order, changes, and operation settings.

Processing layer — runs the actual operation using appropriate libraries or services.

Preview layer — shows page thumbnails, output previews, and document information.

Export layer — handles filenames, output formats, and downloads.

Libraries such as PDF.js and pdf-lib can help with different parts of a browser-based workflow. They aren't interchangeable, though. PDF.js is useful for rendering and inspecting documents, while pdf-lib supports creating and modifying PDFs. More complex features might require other libraries or services.

Don't pretend every operation is identical

There is an important difference between merging two PDFs and editing text inside an existing PDF.

A PDF isn't necessarily a structured Word document with editable paragraphs waiting to be changed. Its content can involve positioned text, embedded fonts, images, vectors, annotations, and other elements.

Trying to turn every PDF editing task into a generic text editor can create broken layouts.

Be honest about supported operations. A reliable page editor is better than a supposedly complete editor that randomly damages document formatting.

Local processing can reduce unnecessary file transfers and improve the experience for certain tasks. But performance matters.

Large scanned files, high-resolution images, and hundreds of pages can put considerable pressure on browser memory.

Use sensible limits, release temporary resources, and avoid keeping unnecessary rendered pages in memory.

Also, explain which operations happen locally and which depend on external processing. Browser-based doesn't automatically mean every operation is local.

Start with document upload, page previews, and a few dependable editing operations. Then add more complex capabilities without forcing them into the primary interface.

A good all-in-one editor should feel like a collection of connected workflows, not a collection of unrelated buttons.

The goal isn't to impress users with the size of the feature list. It's to help them finish their document without opening six different tabs.

What's one PDF editing feature you think deserves a better user experience?
